title: Nervous and Endocrine System Interactions
subject: Nervous System (NEUR)

overview.intro: This chapter explains how the brain runs the endocrine system. The hypothalamus controls the anterior pituitary with hormones carried in portal blood and controls the posterior pituitary with axons that end there, so damage to the hypothalamus, stalk, or sella produces predictable hormonal and visual findings. It then follows two neuroendocrine systems outward: the stress response, with its fast sympathoadrenal arm and slow HPA arm, and thyroid hormone, which builds the developing brain and sets the speed of adult neuromuscular function. Board questions usually describe a sellar mass, a head injury, a postoperative sodium problem, or a reflex finding and ask you to name the structure or hormone responsible.
prerequisites: Hypothalamic nuclei and the gross anatomy of the sella turcica, optic chiasm, and cavernous sinus
Retinotopic organization of the visual pathway and crossing of nasal retinal fibers
Autonomic preganglionic and postganglionic organization and adrenergic receptors (NE-9)
G protein signaling (Gs, Gi, Gq) and nuclear hormone receptor action
Renal water handling in the collecting duct and plasma osmolality

connections.how: The adrenal medulla is a modified sympathetic ganglion, so the fast stress response is ordinary preganglionic sympathetic signaling ending on chromaffin cells.
Because nasal retinal fibers cross in the chiasm just above the sella, an expanding pituitary mass removes the temporal visual fields.
ADH acting on V2 receptors in the collecting duct links hypothalamic injury to serum sodium and urine concentration.
Cytokines such as IL-1, IL-6, and TNF activate the HPA axis, and cortisol in turn suppresses the inflammatory response.
Pituitary adenoma, craniopharyngioma, adrenal insufficiency, and thyroid disease each present with neurological findings explained by the pathways in this chapter.

Small hypothalamic neurons that release releasing and inhibiting hormones into the median eminence.
Large neurons of the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei whose axons carry ADH and oxytocin to the posterior pituitary.
A carrier protein cleaved from the same precursor as ADH or oxytocin that travels with the hormone in secretory granules.
Arcuate nucleus neurons that release dopamine into portal blood to inhibit prolactin secretion tonically.
Mild hyperprolactinemia caused by interruption of dopamine delivery down a compressed or damaged pituitary stalk.
Loss of the temporal half of the visual field in both eyes from damage to crossing fibers in the optic chiasm.
A neural crest derived adrenal medullary cell, equivalent to a postganglionic sympathetic neuron, that secretes catecholamines into blood.
Phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase, the cortisol-induced enzyme that converts norepinephrine to epinephrine in the adrenal medulla.
An enzyme in glial cells that converts T4 to active T3 inside the brain.

sections.title: The hypophyseal portal system and hypothalamic control of the anterior pituitary

blocks.text: The anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis) develops from Rathke pouch, an outgrowth of oral ectoderm, so it has no nerve supply from the hypothalamus. The hypothalamus controls it through blood instead. Parvocellular neurons release small peptides and dopamine into fenestrated capillaries of the median eminence, which lies outside the blood-brain barrier. These capillaries, supplied by the superior hypophyseal arteries from the internal carotid, drain into long portal veins that run down the pituitary stalk and open into a second capillary bed (sinusoids) around the endocrine cells. Most of the anterior lobe's blood arrives this way rather than from a direct artery.

The portal arrangement explains why hypothalamic hormones work in such small amounts. They reach their target before dilution in the systemic circulation, at concentrations far higher than in peripheral blood. It also explains a key weakness: the anterior pituitary depends on an intact stalk for both its signals and much of its blood supply.

blocks.title: Hypothalamic signal to anterior pituitary output
steps: Parvocellular neuron releases hormone in median eminence
Hormone enters fenestrated primary capillary plexus
Long portal veins carry it down the stalk
Secondary capillary plexus bathes anterior pituitary cells
Pituitary hormone enters systemic circulation
Target gland hormone feeds back on hypothalamus and pituitary
blocks.caption: Two capillary beds in series let tiny amounts of hypothalamic hormone act at high concentration.

blocks.title: Hypothalamic hormones that control the anterior pituitary
rows: Raises ACTH (from POMC); ADH acts with it
Raises LH and FSH only when pulsatile
blocks.caption: Four stimulatory and two inhibitory signals; only prolactin is controlled mainly by inhibition.

blocks.text: GnRH illustrates why the pattern of delivery matters. Gonadotrophs respond to pulses, roughly hourly to every few hours depending on cycle phase. Continuous GnRH exposure downregulates and desensitizes its receptors, so LH and FSH fall, which is the mechanism behind the suppressive effect of continuous GnRH agonists.
Why dopamine is the main control of prolactin

Lactotrophs secrete prolactin at a high rate on their own, so their control has to be a brake. Dopamine from tuberoinfundibular neurons acts on D2 receptors, which couple to Gi: cAMP falls, K+ channels open and hyperpolarize the cell, voltage-gated Ca2+ entry drops, and prolactin release, gene transcription, and lactotroph proliferation are all suppressed. Prolactin has no target gland hormone to feed back on it, so it regulates itself by a short loop, raising dopamine output from the same arcuate neurons. Stimulators such as TRH, estrogen, and suckling exist but are secondary. The result is a distinctive rule: if the stalk is cut or the hypothalamus destroyed, every other anterior pituitary hormone falls while prolactin rises. Drugs that block D2 receptors raise prolactin for the same reason, and primary hypothyroidism can raise it through excess TRH.

blocks.predict: A car crash transects the pituitary stalk. Predict the direction of change for GH, ACTH, TSH, LH, FSH, and prolactin.
blocks.explain: Five hormones lose their stimulatory releasing hormone and fall; prolactin loses its dopamine brake and rises.

sections.title: ADH and oxytocin, central diabetes insipidus, and SIADH

blocks.text: The posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis) is a downgrowth of the diencephalon and contains no endocrine cells. Magnocellular neurons in the supraoptic nucleus (SON) and paraventricular nucleus (PVN) make the hormones; ADH (vasopressin) comes mainly from the SON and oxytocin mainly from the PVN, although each nucleus makes some of both. Each hormone is synthesized as a preprohormone with its own carrier protein (neurophysin II with ADH, neurophysin I with oxytocin), packaged into granules, and moved by fast axonal transport down the hypothalamo-hypophyseal tract through the stalk. Granules are stored in swollen axon terminals (Herring bodies) and released by action potential triggered Ca2+ entry into fenestrated capillaries.

blocks.title: ADH response to rising plasma osmolality
steps: Water loss raises plasma osmolality above about 285 mOsm/kg
Hypothalamic osmoreceptors shrink and fire
SON and PVN neurons release ADH from posterior pituitary
ADH binds V2 receptors, Gs raises cAMP
Aquaporin-2 inserts into collecting duct apical membrane
Water is reabsorbed and osmolality falls
blocks.caption: Osmoreceptors near the lamina terminalis respond to changes of about 1%; a fall in blood volume of roughly 5 to 10% is needed before baroreceptors become a strong stimulus.

blocks.text: Oxytocin contracts myoepithelial cells for milk ejection, a neuroendocrine reflex triggered by suckling, and uterine smooth muscle in labor, where cervical stretch drives a positive feedback loop. ADH also constricts vessels through V1 receptors (Gq), which matters mainly in severe hypovolemia.
How CNS injury disturbs ADH

Central diabetes insipidus (DI) is too little ADH. The collecting duct stays impermeable to water, so large volumes of dilute urine (usually below about 300 mOsm/kg) are lost. Thirst usually compensates, so serum sodium is high normal; it rises clearly when the patient cannot drink or the thirst center is also damaged. Causes include head trauma, pituitary surgery, craniopharyngioma, and infiltrative or metastatic disease of the stalk. Permanent DI requires loss of most magnocellular cell bodies, so a high stalk or hypothalamic lesion is more likely to be permanent, while a low stalk lesion often recovers because cut axons can release ADH from their proximal ends. When ADH is given, urine concentrates in central DI but not in nephrogenic DI, which locates the defect.

SIADH is ADH secretion that persists despite low plasma osmolality. Water is retained, serum sodium falls, and urine stays inappropriately concentrated. Patients look euvolemic because the modest volume expansion triggers natriuresis, so urine sodium stays high. CNS causes include head trauma, subarachnoid hemorrhage, meningitis, encephalitis, stroke, and tumors; small cell lung cancer is the classic ectopic source. Falling osmolality draws water into brain cells, causing headache, confusion, and seizures. Cerebral salt wasting after subarachnoid hemorrhage also gives hyponatremia with high urine sodium, but the patient is volume depleted.

blocks.title: Central DI and SIADH compared
blocks.caption: Plasma and urine osmolality read together locate the problem; one value alone does not.

blocks.title: Worked example: sodium after pituitary surgery
blocks.text: After transsphenoidal surgery, a patient passes large volumes of dilute urine on day 1 with sodium 147 mEq/L. Injured axons have stopped conducting, so ADH release fails (phase 1, DI). Around day 6, urine output drops and sodium falls to 128 mEq/L despite normal volume. Degenerating terminals are now leaking their stored ADH without regulation (phase 2, SIADH pattern). Once the stores are exhausted, polyuria returns and persists if most SON and PVN cell bodies have died (phase 3, permanent DI). Each phase follows from where ADH is made, stored, and released.

sections.title: Sellar masses: chiasmal compression and the stalk effect

blocks.text: The pituitary sits in the sella turcica, roofed by the diaphragma sellae. The optic chiasm lies above the diaphragma, separated from it by the suprasellar cistern, and the hypothalamus and third ventricle lie just behind and above the chiasm. The cavernous sinuses flank the sella; CN III, CN IV, V1, and V2 run in their lateral walls, and CN VI and the internal carotid artery run through them. A mass's direction of growth therefore predicts its signs.
Visual field loss

In the chiasm, fibers from the nasal hemiretinas cross. Nasal retina sees the temporal field, so midline compression removes both temporal fields (bitemporal hemianopia) while sparing the uncrossed temporal retinal fibers. Inferior crossing fibers come from the inferior nasal retina, which sees the upper temporal field. A pituitary adenoma growing up from below presses these first, so loss begins in the upper temporal quadrants. A craniopharyngioma often presses from above and can begin with lower temporal loss. Because loss is gradual and central vision is spared early, patients often notice it late. If the chiasm sits unusually far forward or back, the same mass may compress an optic tract (homonymous hemianopia) or an optic nerve (monocular loss).

blocks.title: Pituitary adenoma and craniopharyngioma compared
rows: Childhood peak and a second peak in older adults
Monomorphic cells; macroadenoma 10 mm or more
Adamantinomatous (children): cysts, calcification, CTNNB1; papillary (adults): BRAF V600E
Common: DI, growth failure, obesity, hydrocephalus
blocks.caption: Diabetes insipidus at presentation points away from a plain adenoma, because an adenoma rarely damages the hypothalamus or high stalk.

blocks.text: Hormonal effects and the stalk effect

A nonfunctioning mass compresses the normal gland and the portal vessels, producing hypopituitarism, classically with GH and gonadotropins failing first and ACTH last. Compression of the stalk also blocks dopamine delivery, so lactotrophs are released from inhibition and prolactin rises, usually only mildly. Raised prolactin suppresses pulsatile GnRH release (largely through hypothalamic kisspeptin neurons), causing amenorrhea, infertility, galactorrhea, low libido, and erectile dysfunction. A prolactinoma, the most common hormone-secreting adenoma, produces prolactin in proportion to its size, so a large mass with only mild hyperprolactinemia suggests stalk effect.

blocks.title: Stalk effect
steps: Sellar mass compresses pituitary stalk
Dopamine delivery in portal blood falls
Lactotrophs lose D2 inhibition
Prolactin rises modestly
Prolactin suppresses pulsatile GnRH
LH and FSH fall, causing hypogonadism
blocks.caption: A nonfunctioning mass can produce galactorrhea and amenorrhea through loss of dopamine inhibition alone.

blocks.title: Worked example: adenoma or stalk effect?
blocks.text: A man has headaches, bitemporal field loss, low libido, and a 3 cm sellar mass. Prolactin is about 60 ng/mL (normal roughly 20 or less). A prolactinoma this large would usually push prolactin into the hundreds or thousands, because output tracks tumor mass. A level this modest fits a nonfunctioning adenoma blocking dopamine flow down the stalk, with low gonadotropins from compression and prolactin-induced GnRH suppression. One caution: an extremely high prolactin can saturate the immunoassay and read falsely low (hook effect), so a large mass with a modest level is often retested on a diluted sample.

A stressor, whether hemorrhage, hypoglycemia, infection, pain, or fear, reaches the hypothalamus through brainstem visceral pathways, the amygdala, and circulating cytokines. The paraventricular nucleus (PVN) then drives two outputs that differ in speed because one is neural and the other is a hormonal cascade.

In the fast arm, PVN and other hypothalamic neurons project to brainstem sympathetic centers and directly to preganglionic neurons in the intermediolateral cell column of the thoracolumbar cord. Preganglionic fibers in the splanchnic nerves pass through the sympathetic chain without synapsing and end directly on adrenal medullary chromaffin cells. These neural crest derived cells are modified postganglionic neurons: acetylcholine opens their nicotinic receptors, Ca2+ enters, and catecholamines are released into blood within seconds, about 80% epinephrine and 20% norepinephrine. Epinephrine raises heart rate and contractility (beta 1), dilates bronchi and skeletal muscle vessels (beta 2), and mobilizes fuel through glycogenolysis and lipolysis, while alpha 2 effects on beta cells hold insulin down.

In the slow arm (the HPA axis), parvocellular PVN neurons release CRH, often with ADH, which strengthens the response. In the anterior pituitary, CRH acts through Gs to stimulate corticotrophs, which cleave POMC to ACTH. ACTH binds MC2R in the zona fasciculata; cAMP increases StAR-mediated cholesterol transport to the inner mitochondrial membrane, the rate-limiting step. Cortisol is not stored, so its rise lags ACTH by minutes.

blocks.title: The two arms of the stress response
rows: Hypothalamus, preganglionic sympathetic fibers, adrenal medulla
PVN, CRH in portal blood, ACTH, adrenal cortex
Intracellular glucocorticoid receptor changes gene transcription
Cardiac output, bronchodilation, glucose and fatty acid release
Gluconeogenesis, protein catabolism, permissive vascular tone, anti-inflammation
blocks.caption: The neural arm meets an emergency; the hormonal arm sustains fuel supply and circulation.

blocks.text: Cortisol raises glucose through hepatic gluconeogenesis supplied by muscle protein breakdown and lipolysis. It is permissive for catecholamines, maintaining adrenergic receptor expression and vascular responsiveness. It suppresses inflammation by inducing annexin A1, which limits phospholipase A2, and by inhibiting NF-kappa B, which lowers IL-1, IL-2, and TNF production. Cortisol also feeds back on the PVN, corticotrophs, and hippocampus to end the response.

The arms are linked anatomically and chemically. Blood draining the cortex carries high cortisol into the medulla, where it induces PNMT, the enzyme that converts norepinephrine to epinephrine; that is why the medulla secretes mostly epinephrine. CRH activates the locus coeruleus, and norepinephrine stimulates CRH neurons, so each arm reinforces the other. When cortisol is absent, as in adrenal insufficiency, catecholamines lose much of their vascular effect and stress can cause shock that resists pressors. When the axis stays active for weeks, sustained cortisol produces hyperglycemia, muscle wasting, immunosuppression, and hypertension.

blocks.title: HPA axis negative feedback
steps: Stressor activates PVN CRH neurons
CRH reaches corticotrophs through portal blood
Corticotrophs release ACTH
Zona fasciculata synthesizes cortisol
Cortisol inhibits CRH and ACTH release
blocks.caption: Cortisol shuts off its own drive; loss of this feedback raises ACTH in primary adrenal failure.

blocks.predict: A patient on long-term glucocorticoid therapy has surgery. Predict the adrenal cortex response to the stress.
blocks.explain: Prolonged feedback suppression of CRH and ACTH atrophies the zona fasciculata, so cortisol cannot rise and catecholamine responses lose their permissive support.

sections.title: Thyroid hormone and the nervous system

blocks.text: Thyroid hormone acts on the brain mainly as T3, but most of that T3 is made inside the brain. T4 crosses the blood-brain barrier on transporters (including MCT8 and OATP1C1), and type 2 deiodinase in glial cells (astrocytes and tanycytes, third ventricle glia) converts it to T3, which then enters neurons. Neurons express type 3 deiodinase, which inactivates T3. This local control lets the brain keep T3 relatively stable when serum T4 changes. T3 binds nuclear thyroid hormone receptors, mainly TR alpha 1 in the brain, which pair with the retinoid X receptor on thyroid response elements and change transcription of genes for neuronal migration, dendrite and axon growth, synapse formation, and myelin proteins.
Congenital hypothyroidism

These gene programs run during a critical period from late fetal life through about the first two to three years. In the first trimester the fetus depends on maternal T4; the fetal thyroid begins making hormone at about 10 to 12 weeks. A newborn without a working thyroid still receives some maternal T4 through the placenta, so cord blood T4 is roughly 25 to 50% of normal and the baby often looks normal at birth. Damage accumulates after delivery, when that supply is gone. Early signs are lethargy, poor feeding, prolonged jaundice, hypotonia, macroglossia, umbilical hernia, and a large posterior fontanelle. If the deficit continues through the critical period, the result is permanent intellectual disability and short stature, because neurons that missed their window of growth and myelination cannot recover it later. This is why newborns are screened. In iodine-sufficient regions most cases come from thyroid dysgenesis; worldwide, iodine deficiency remains the leading preventable cause of intellectual disability.

blocks.title: Why congenital hypothyroidism damages the brain permanently
steps: Neonatal thyroid fails; maternal T4 supply ends at birth
Brain T3 falls despite increased deiodinase activity
Fewer TR alpha 1 target genes are transcribed
Dendrite growth, synapse formation, and myelination slow
Critical period closes
Permanent intellectual disability
blocks.caption: The timing of the deficit, not its severity alone, decides whether the damage is reversible.

blocks.text: Adult hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism

In the adult brain, thyroid hormone no longer builds circuits, so its effects are on speed and arousal. The most testable sign is the delayed relaxation phase of the deep tendon reflex in hypothyroidism. The cause is in muscle, not nerve: T3 normally drives expression of SERCA, the sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca2+ pump, and fast myosin isoforms. With less T3, Ca2+ is pumped back slowly and cross-bridges detach slowly, so the limb returns slowly after a normal jerk. In hyperthyroidism the reverse occurs, and T3 also increases beta-adrenergic receptor number and responsiveness. Catecholamine levels are normal or low, yet sympathetic effects are exaggerated, producing a fine, fast postural tremor, brisk reflexes, anxiety, and insomnia.

blocks.title: Neurological effects of thyroid hormone excess and deficiency
rows: Myopathy with cramps and raised CK
Proximal weakness; rare hypokalemic periodic paralysis
Carpal tunnel syndrome from myxedematous tissue
Hyponatremia from impaired free water excretion; high TRH can raise prolactin
Low TSH (about 0.4 to 4.0 mU/L normal) with high free T4
blocks.caption: Most adult findings reflect altered metabolic rate, Ca2+ handling in muscle, and beta-adrenergic sensitivity rather than structural brain injury.

blocks.predict: An adult who develops severe hypothyroidism and a newborn with untreated congenital hypothyroidism both have low T3 for one year. Predict which brain changes will reverse when thyroid hormone is restored.
blocks.explain: The adult's slowing reverses because the circuits are already built; the infant's deficits largely persist because the critical period for growth and myelination has passed.
blocks.check: Compare with the congenital hypothyroidism flow and the paragraph on adult effects.

integration.text: Anatomy and embryology explain most of this chapter. The anterior pituitary comes from oral ectoderm and receives no axons, so it depends on portal blood, while the posterior pituitary is brain tissue that only stores hormone, so injury at different levels of the stalk produces different syndromes. The chiasm above the sella turns a pituitary mass into a visual field problem, and the adrenal medulla, built from neural crest, is effectively a sympathetic ganglion that secretes into blood. Renal physiology and immunology complete the picture: ADH errors appear as serum sodium disorders, and cytokines drive the HPA axis that cortisol uses to restrain inflammation.

Laboratory cutoffs for prolactin, sodium, and osmolality vary between laboratories and sources, field defects do not always follow textbook order because chiasm position varies, and the triphasic ADH response after surgery is a pattern only some patients complete. Reason from mechanism first, then check the value against the stated reference range.

summary: Parvocellular hypothalamic hormones enter fenestrated median eminence capillaries and reach the anterior pituitary through portal veins at high concentration.
TRH, CRH, GnRH (pulsatile), and GHRH stimulate; somatostatin inhibits GH and TSH, and dopamine through D2 and Gi is the main control of prolactin.
Cutting the stalk lowers every anterior pituitary hormone except prolactin, which rises.
ADH (mainly SON) and oxytocin (mainly PVN) travel with neurophysins down axons and are released from the posterior pituitary.
Central DI gives dilute polyuria and high normal to high sodium; SIADH gives euvolemic hyponatremia with inappropriately concentrated urine and high urine sodium.
Pituitary surgery or stalk injury can produce DI, then an SIADH pattern from leaking terminals, then permanent DI.
Midline chiasm compression causes bitemporal hemianopia; adenomas from below take the upper temporal fields first.
Mild hyperprolactinemia with a large mass suggests stalk effect; prolactinoma levels track tumor size.
The stress response pairs seconds-fast epinephrine from chromaffin cells with slower cortisol from the HPA axis; cortisol induces PNMT and is permissive for catecholamines.

Brain T3 is made locally by type 2 deiodinase; congenital deficiency causes permanent intellectual disability, while adult hypothyroidism slows reflex relaxation and hyperthyroidism causes tremor and hyperreflexia.

verify: Osmotic threshold for ADH release is quoted from about 280 to 290 mOsm/kg, and the volume loss needed for a strong baroreceptor stimulus from about 5 to 15%; values here are approximate.
Timing of the triphasic response (phase 1 in the first days, phase 2 around days 5 to 10, phase 3 thereafter) varies between sources and patients.
SIADH urine sodium cutoff is given as above 30 or above 40 mEq/L depending on the source; confirm the value NABNE uses.
Prolactin reference limits and the level that separates stalk effect from macroprolactinoma (often quoted as about 100 to 150 versus about 200 to 250 ng/mL) vary by laboratory and text.
The order of hormone loss in compressive hypopituitarism (GH and gonadotropins first, ACTH last) is classic teaching but not invariable.
Craniopharyngioma age peaks are quoted as about 5 to 14 years and about 50 to 74 years in some sources and about 45 to 60 years in others.
The adrenal medullary epinephrine to norepinephrine ratio is quoted as about 80:20 in most texts and 85:15 in some.
Cord blood T4 in athyreotic newborns (about 25 to 50% of normal) and the length of the critical period (about 2 to 3 years) are consensus approximations.
Confirm whether NABNE Part I expects the terms Herring bodies, Woltman sign (delayed reflex relaxation), and hook effect, or only the descriptive findings.
